summary: This paper presents a hardware-grounded distributed architecture for fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computation and a comprehensive resource-estimation protocol for surface-code-based modular processors connected via noisy inter-chip links. Using RSA-2048 factorization as a benchmark under experimentally anchored parameters ($p_b = 10^{-3}$, $p_s = 10^{-2}$, inter-chip gates up to $25 	imes$ slower), the distributed architecture requires only 2.0 million physical qubits and 4.4 days compared to a monolithic baseline of 1.3 million qubits and 3.4 days, with overhead nearly scale-invariant across module capacities from thousands to hundreds of thousands qubits per chip.
motivation: Scaling fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computers to utility scale requires multiple manufacturable quantum processing units rather than monolithic chips, but the impact of noisy and slow inter-chip operations on spacetime overhead and system complexity remains unclear.
method: The authors developed a latency-decoupled syndrome-extraction protocol with buffer qubits that confines slow inter-chip operations to module boundaries, decoupling intra-chip and inter-chip QEC cycles, combined with a three-layer resource-estimation procedure integrating physical error models, QEC code specifications, and algorithmic workload across computation and memory zones.
result: Under baseline error rates, the distributed architecture incurs only 60% additional physical-qubit overhead and 30% additional runtime compared to monolithic, with surface-code distance increasing modestly from $d = 27$ to $d = 31$; crucially, this overhead remains nearly independent of chip capacity across an experimentally relevant window ($10^3$–$2 	imes 10^5$ qubits per chip), decoupling module size from global performance penalties.
